1261.title: Wesley's warmed heart
1261.hook: faith as a living trust you can feel, leading to holy love
1261.howItsDone: Methodist and other Wesleyan Christians remember Wesley's Aldersgate experience, meet in small groups for prayer and accountability, and teach growth in holy love; across churches, Christians speak of faith as heartfelt trust shown in love of neighbor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Edwards on beauty: every lovely thing an echo. Your line was God is beautiful.

"In the evening I went very unwillingly to a society in Aldersgate Street." That's how John Wesley, whom you met in year three, begins the story in his journal. He's an Anglican priest. He has prayed, fasted, preached and served the poor, and still he doubts he has the faith he preaches. At the meeting, someone is reading aloud from Luther's preface to Paul's letter to the Romans. And Wesley writes what happened next: "I felt my heart strangely warmed."

The journal goes on: "I felt I did trust in Christ, Christ alone, for salvation." Notice what's new. Wesley already knew and preached the faith. What came that evening was trust he could feel, an assurance in the heart. For Wesley, faith isn't only agreeing that certain statements are true. It's a living trust in God that the heart can know. But the warmed heart was a beginning, not an ending. Wesley went on to preach in fields and town squares, to gather people into small groups that prayed together and kept one another honest, and to teach what he called holiness. And holiness, for Wesley, meant love: loving God with all your heart, and your neighbor as yourself, the commands Jesus calls the first and the second. Wesley hoped that by God's grace that love could grow until it filled a whole life. Other Christians questioned how far he pressed that hope. Methodist and other Wesleyan churches carry his teaching on. The Bible has its own warmed hearts. Two disciples walk to Emmaus with a stranger who turns out to be the risen Jesus, and afterward they say to each other: "Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way?" And the letter to the Hebrews says: "Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord." Wesley held those two together. The heart is warmed, and then the warmth goes to work. A feeling that never reached a neighbor, for him, would have missed the point.

Put a hand on your chest if you like, feel it rise and fall, and ask gently what's here: warmth, coldness, tiredness, longing, nothing much. Wesley went to that meeting unwillingly, so whatever you bring is enough to notice, without fixing or judging it. If you pray, you can offer what you find to God, without dressing it up.
Wesley's warmed heart. Faith as a living trust you can feel, which, for Wesley, grows into holy love of God and neighbor.
Your line: heart and holiness. The warmth goes to work. Until tomorrow.

1262.title: Schleiermacher
1262.hook: religion as the feeling of absolute dependence
1262.howItsDone: Christians who draw on Schleiermacher often describe prayer less as asking and more as resting in awareness of God as the source of all things; his thought is studied in Protestant seminaries and debated across the churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Wesley's warmed heart: faith as a living trust you can feel, growing into holy love. Your line was heart and holiness.

A short experiment. Name one thing in this minute that you made yourself. The breath you just took came without asking. Your heartbeat started before you knew your own name. The floor under you, the light in the room, the language you're thinking in: all handed to you. Friedrich Schleiermacher, a German preacher and professor, pointed at that kind of givenness. He wrote a book for educated friends who thought religion was finished, a pile of old rules and stale arguments. They were looking in the wrong place, he said. Religion begins deeper down, in a kind of feeling.

In his book The Christian Faith, Schleiermacher names the heart of religion in one phrase, usually given in English as the feeling of absolute dependence. Feeling: not a mood like happy or sad, but an awareness underneath the moods, a sense of where you stand. Dependence: we know the partial kind all the time. You depend on the bus, a paycheck, a friend, and you push back on the world a little: you choose, you act, you change things. That freedom is real. But in one relation, he says, the push only goes one way. Your whole self, your freedom included, comes from somewhere you didn't make. That's absolute dependence, and the word God, for him, names the one we depend on in that way. The Bible has its own words for it. Paul, speaking in Athens, says of God: "For in him we live, and move, and have our being." A psalm pictures every creature waiting on God: "These wait all upon thee; that thou mayest give them their meat in due season." Schleiermacher had sharp critics. Some said he turned faith into a mood, moving the center from God speaking to humans feeling; Karl Barth, whom this path meets again soon, argued with him hard. His defenders answer that he meant something steadier: the plain fact of being held, finally noticed. Christians still argue about where he leads. But his question stays a fair one: before any argument, what is it like to be a creature?

1263.title: Kierkegaard's individual
1263.hook: each person stands before God alone, not as part of a crowd
1263.howItsDone: Christians shaped by Kierkegaard often stress personal decision and honest self-examination before God, alongside life in a church; his books are read by Protestants, Catholics and readers of no faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Schleiermacher: religion beginning in the feeling of absolute dependence. Your line was entirely held.

A stadium rises to its feet before anyone has decided anything. A group chat piles onto someone, and it's oddly easy to add one more laughing face. A crowd can carry a person a long way without asking a single question. In Copenhagen, Søren Kierkegaard, the Danish writer this path met earlier, watched this happen in the newspapers, in the streets, and, he thought, in the churches too. So he did something odd for an author. He dedicated some of his books not to a crowd of readers, but to one: that single individual, whoever you are, reading alone.

His sharp sentence for it is usually put in English as: the crowd is untruth. He didn't mean people in groups are bad. He meant a crowd lets each person hide. In a crowd nobody quite decides; everyone goes along, and nobody quite answers for it. Against the crowd he set a picture from the Bible: each person standing before God, alone. Paul writes to the Romans: "So then every one of us shall give account of himself to God." Every one. Of himself. Not as a member of a nation, a family, or even a congregation. In Fear and Trembling he dwells on Abraham on the mountain, called by name, and answering, "Here am I." No committee. One voice, one answer. Kierkegaard wasn't against church or neighbors; he wrote a whole book, Works of Love, about loving the neighbor. His point was that nobody can hold your faith for you. Growing up in a country that called itself Christian, he thought, didn't make anyone a Christian by itself; each person had to become one, with their own yes. Some Christians find this bracing. Others worry it leaves too little room for the church as one body, and point out how often scripture says "we." Both readings are alive today. But the picture he left is hard to shake: before God, there's no back row to hide in.
screen: `THE CROWD IS UNTRUTH` · `EACH ONE GIVES ACCOUNT` · `ABRAHAM: HERE AM I` · `NO BACK ROW BEFORE GOD`

1264.title: Newman on development
1264.hook: doctrine grows like a seed, staying itself while changing
1264.howItsDone: Catholic teaching often speaks of doctrine developing over time while staying faithful to the apostles, and Newman is studied in that light; other churches discuss the same question in their own ways, through scripture, councils and tradition.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kierkegaard's individual: each person standing before God, with no crowd to hide in. Your line was before God, alone.

A baby photo stuck to a fridge. Everything about that child has changed since: the height, the voice, the things that make them laugh. Yet nobody at the kitchen table doubts it's the same person. John Henry Newman, an English priest and writer, needed that puzzle for a bigger question. Christian teaching seemed to have changed down the centuries: new words, new feasts, new definitions the apostles never wrote down. Had the church drifted away from where it started? Or had it grown up? Newman wrote a long essay to find out.

His answer came from the garden. A true idea, he said, is alive. It grows the way a seed grows into a tree, unfolding what was in it from the start. An oak doesn't look like an acorn, but it's the same living thing, and nothing in the oak contradicts the seed. Jesus used this kind of picture: the kingdom of heaven is "like to a grain of mustard seed," sown small, grown into a tree where the birds come and lodge in its branches. Paul too: "I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase." Newman also wrote a sentence people still quote, and today's line comes from it: "In a higher world it is otherwise, but here below to live is to change, and to be perfect is to have changed often." He isn't praising every change. Much of his essay asks how to tell true growth from corruption. Does the new thing keep the same type, the same shape of life? Does it carry the earlier teaching forward, or quietly cancel it? A tumor grows too. Newman wrote this while moving from the Church of England into the Catholic Church, so the question was his own. Christians still weigh his answer differently. Catholic theologians have drawn on him to explain how teaching unfolds over time; Orthodox and Protestant Christians ask their own hard questions about which developments truly grew from the seed. His puzzle reaches past any one church: how does something living change and stay itself?

1265.title: Sobornost
1265.hook: Khomiakov: the church as free unity in love
1265.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians often speak of the church's life as conciliar: bishops meet in councils, and the faith is understood to be held by the whole people of God together, not by any one person alone.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Newman on development: teaching that grows like a seed, changing and staying itself. Your line was to live is to change.

A tense meeting in Jerusalem. Followers of Jesus who aren't Jewish are joining, and believers disagree about what to ask of them. Paul and Barnabas have already argued it out in Antioch. So the apostles and elders gather. Peter speaks. The whole room goes quiet and listens to Barnabas and Paul. James speaks. At last they send out a letter with an unusual line in it: "For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us." Not one voice ruling. Not the loudest side winning. A Russian thinker named Alexei Khomiakov built his whole picture of the church around that kind of togetherness.
screen: `IT SEEMED GOOD TO THE SPIRIT, AND TO US.`

segments.voice: Sobornost is a Russian word with no neat English match. Translators try conciliarity, or togetherness, or catholicity in its old sense of wholeness. Tradition ties it to sobor, a word for a gathering, a council, or a cathedral. Khomiakov used it for the church as a free unity in love. Hold both halves. Unity: the church isn't a pile of separate believers who happen to share a building. It's one life, like the believers in Acts, who "were of one heart and of one soul." Freely: that unity can't be forced, not by a ruler, not by fear, not by pressure. The truth, Khomiakov said, isn't kept by any one person alone, but by the whole church together, bound in love, and love keeps the knowing safe. He set this against two shortcuts he saw in the Western churches: Rome, to him, held unity without enough freedom, and Protestants kept freedom without enough unity. Catholic and Protestant Christians describe their own churches differently, and wouldn't accept that picture of them; Orthodox writers since have debated it too. But they still use the word for something hard: being many and one at once. Set it beside Kierkegaard's crowd, where nobody answers for anything. Sobornost isn't a crowd at all: a body where every person answers freely, and still they answer together.
screen: `A WORD WITH NO ENGLISH MATCH` · `ONE HEART AND ONE SOUL` · `UNITY THAT CAN'T BE FORCED` · `NOT A CROWD, A BODY`

1266.title: Soloviev
1266.hook: a Russian philosopher who longed for the reunion of the churches
1266.howItsDone: Christians of different churches pray for unity in their own services, and some gather each year for shared prayer for Christian unity; Orthodox, Catholic and Protestant leaders also meet in ongoing dialogue.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sobornost: Khomiakov's picture of the church as a free unity in love. Your line was together, freely.

A strange story ends in the wilderness. The world has fallen under a smooth, charming ruler who offers everyone exactly what they want, and the world takes the deal. The few Christians who refuse him gather outside, with three leaders at their head: an Orthodox elder named John, a pope named Peter, and a Protestant scholar named Pauli. Peter, John and Paul. Near the story's end, those three churches become one again. The man who wrote that tale was Vladimir Soloviev, a Russian Orthodox philosopher, and the ending wasn't decoration. It was the thing he longed for.

Soloviev was a philosopher and a poet, and much of his thinking circled one wound: the split between the churches of East and West, which this path met earlier. He didn't treat it as a technical problem for committees. He treated it as a break in a family. A prayer of Jesus in John's Gospel, spoken on the night before he died, names the hope he kept circling: "That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us." He also wrote about what he called Godmanhood: God and humanity coming together, first in Christ, and then, he hoped, drawing all of humanity into one shared life. A divided church, to him, was that life torn down the middle. He loved his own Orthodox church, and he also wrote warmly of Rome, and some on both sides were uneasy with him for it. Christians today hold different hopes for what unity would mean: shared communion, shared leadership, or a deep friendship that leaves real differences standing. His tale doesn't settle that. It does something quieter. It puts the names of three apostles on three churches and lets them stand side by side in the dark, refusing the same false ruler, recognizing each other at last. Readers still argue over what the scene says about Rome. But the picture it leaves is a family back together.
screen: `A WOUND BETWEEN EAST AND WEST` · `THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE` · `GODMANHOOD: GOD AND HUMANITY JOINED` · `NOT A VICTORY, A REUNION`

1267.title: Chesterton's fairyland
1267.hook: Chesterton, in Orthodoxy (1908), argues life is a strange gift like a fairy tale
1267.howItsDone: Christians who love Chesterton often read Orthodoxy as a book of gratitude and wonder rather than argument alone; churches also give thanks for creation in their prayers, and some Christians say grace before meals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Soloviev, who longed for the churches of East and West to be one family again. Your line was all one.

Why is grass green? A small child asks, and the grown-up has an answer ready. Then the child asks why again, and again, until the grown-up runs out and says: it just is. The English writer G. K. Chesterton thought that last answer deserved a much longer look. In his book Orthodoxy there's a chapter called The Ethics of Elfland, and it starts in the nursery, with the fairy tales of his childhood. Those stories, he says, taught him something about the real world that grown-up books had missed.

In fairyland, nobody pretends a golden apple had to be golden. It's magic: someone chose it. Chesterton turns that around on the world outside the window. We call it a law that apples fall and leaves are green, and the word law makes it sound necessary, as if it couldn't have been any other way. But we don't actually know why it's this way and not another. A world where grass happens to be green is a world someone might have chosen. Then he goes a step further. We tend to think repetition means something is dead, like a machine. Chesterton suggests the opposite. A laughing child says "Do it again!" and means it every single time. Perhaps, he says, God makes each daisy separately and has never grown tired of making them, with the strength of a child who wants the same game over and over. Jesus pointed somewhere nearby: "Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven." And the psalmist, looking out at creation, doesn't explain it at all. He marvels: "O LORD, how manifold are thy works! in wisdom hast thou made them all." Chesterton's point isn't that the world is a fable. It's that the world is stranger than a fable, and that being alive at all is a gift nobody earned. And a gift, he says, leaves you wanting someone to thank.

segments.voice: Pick one plain thing within reach, a spoon, a key, a slice of bread, and look at it as if you'd stepped into a story and this was the first one you'd ever seen: why this color, this shape, why here at all? Don't answer; let it be strange for a while. If you pray, you can borrow the psalmist's line: O Lord, how manifold are thy works.
Chesterton's fairyland. G. K. Chesterton's idea that the ordinary world is as strange and chosen as a fairy tale, and calls for thanks.
Your line: the world is strange. That closes a week of thinkers, from Wesley's warm heart to Chesterton's wonder. I'll be here tomorrow.

chat.says: Chesterton and fairyland? Was he saying religion is just a fairy tale?
options: No. He said the real world is as strange as a fairy tale, and a gift that calls for thanks.
Yes. He said faith is a lovely story that grown-ups should keep just for the children.
No. He said fairy tales are harmful, and children should read only plain real facts.
